mod1 <- mirt(data,2)

However, mod1 and mod 2 are not equivalent. How can this be?

Regards,

Kornelius

messages.body_plain:
Hugo is correct, these models are numerically equivalent to each other (you can use anova(mod1, mod2) to verify the likelihood information as well). Numeral optimizer often work slightly differently depending on the starting values (including ordering due to the computation of a quasi-Hessian in the quasi-Newton updates), so this is driven by the M-step updates. But, if you wan the solutions to be even more similar, just decrease the TOL input to something even smaller, like TOL=1e-8.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Plotting coefficients in mixedmirt, and unipolar item response models
messages.subject_clean: Plotting coefficients in mixedmirt, and unipolar item response models
messages.body_plain:
These models could be fit in mirt using some of the customized input methods. Namely, the createItem() and createGroup() function to build these customized IRT probability models (the former), and specifying a log-normal prior density function for theta (the latter). You'd also need to provide a new Theta grid to integrate over since negative thetas in the quadrature grid would not be valid under these models. Estimation will be fairly slow given that numerical derivatives and such will be used (unless you provide the derivative functions yourself....in which case feel free to contact me since I'd be willing to add these models into the core package if the Hessian and gradient code were already written). Not sure about starting values for these models, but you may know more about what will be reasonable for  your datasets anyway. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Standardized item residuals
messages.body_plain:
That's not what Templin is referring to, unfortunately. I believe his notes pertain to the classical X2 statistics, which are generally less useful these days. These require computing the proportion of responses given a *binned* theta, and determining a goodness-of-fit statistics based on these binned data terms. This is available in the itemfit() function, in addition to having the plots generated for the same data. But, note that these are generally not very good fit statistics unless the test length is extremely long; otherwise, they are quite liberal representations of misfit.

library(mirt)
dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)
mod <- mirt(dat, 1)
itemfit(mod, fit_stats = 'X2', method = 'ML')
itemfit(mod, empirical.plot = 1, method = 'ML')

Phil

The plotting functions in mirt are unfortunately limited to the theta metric and cannot be changed for numerical reasons. messages.subject: Re: Covariance estimation in bifactor model?
messages.body_plain:
The bfactor() function imposes a orthogonal structure on the specific factors. Hence, providing covariance parameters other than 0 will just be ignored (this should probably throw an error, but it is documented in the function nonetheless).

That said, would this model even be identified? The global covariation between the specific factors would be absorbed by the G factor. At best I think you can correlate some of the specific factors in a bifactor structure, but not all of them. And in this case, the bfactor() function wouldn't be appropriate, so you couldn't estimate the model using the dimension-reduction algorithms provided.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
I see. Well part of the issue here is that fscores() does not have a covdata input, so whatever is happening is not supporting that input. The other thing though is that the object supplied to fscores() is a single group latent regression model, where internally the covariates and response data are stored separately. Hence, overriding one input requires overriding the other in order to make any sense.

What you're seeing from the successful fscores() run is the conditional EAP scores, where the latent regression effects are already included for each response pattern. Supplying different response patterns and covdata inputs is a bit more awkward because you technically need to create a new fitted model object with the associated response patterns and data, where the IRT parameter estimates are fixed at the previously estimated values from the first model (clunky, I know, but that's the best option for now). I could add support for the response.pattern + covdata inputs at a later time though, which would save this two-step approach. But for now it doesn't seem that essential given the workaround. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Setting $est all to FALSE implies that no parameters are estimated in the model; hence, you have many more degrees of freedom because you are assuming these parameters are actually fixed and known a priori. As statistics like M2 are based on an orthogonal compliment from the estimated parameters, setting all to FALSE is really not true since you really meant for these elements to be estimated an not known. Ultimately, this just means that you're implying less sampling variability than there really was.

If you insist on doing things like this, try not setting $est to FALSE and just leave these as is. But, pass TOL = NaN or TOL = NA to force the model to instantly converge (the differences between these two is whether you want the log-likelihood to be evaluated or not). Then, M2 and other fit stats should work more as expected. HTH.

Phil
